Question 1
?

Find the particular solution to the differential equation dydx=y2x2+1 that satisfies y(1)=1.

a
y=1π−4+4arctan⁡(x)
b
y=1π+1−arctan⁡(x)
c
y=4π−1−arctan⁡(x)
d
y=4π+4−4arctan⁡(x)
e
y=2π+2−4arctan⁡(x)
Submit

decision.explanation: Separating variables and integrating gives -1/y=arctan(x)+C. Since y(1)=1, C=-1-π/4. Thus y=4/(π+4-4arctan(x)), which is option d.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}$  that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
after.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C \\ \frac{1}{y} & =-(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C}.
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)+C} \\ 1 & =-\frac{1}{\frac{\pi }{4}+C} \\ C & =-\frac{\pi }{4}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)-\frac{\pi }{4}-1}=\frac{4}{\pi +4-4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)}.
$$

a

We conclude that the general solution is y=−1arctan⁡(x)+C. where C is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition y(1)=1 to find C:

1=−1arctan⁡(1)+C1=−1π4+CC=−π4−1

content.knowledge_point: Finding Particular Solutions of Differential Equations by Separating the Variables
content.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}$  that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
content.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1} \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C \\ \frac{1}{y} & =-(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the general solution is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+C}.
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1)+C} \\ 1 & =-\frac{1}{\frac{\pi }{4}+C} \\ C & =-\frac{\pi }{4}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+1}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y=-\frac{1}{\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)-\frac{\pi }{4}-1}=\frac{4}{\pi +4-4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)}.
$$

decision.explanation: Separate variables: (ln(y)/y) dy = -x dx. Integrating gives (ln(y))²/2 = -x²/2 + C. Using y(0)=e gives C=1/2, so (ln(y))²=1-x², option d. The initial condition selects y=exp(sqrt(1-x²)) for -1<x<1.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{xy}{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}$ that satisfies $y(0)=e.$
after.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find the particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{xy}{\operatorname{ln}⁡y} \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-x \\ \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\,\text{d}y & =-\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\text{d}y & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the integral in the left-hand side of this equality, we use a substitution $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡y.$ Then,  we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=\frac{1}{y}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y.
$$

So we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{ln}⁡y(\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\int u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{ln}^{2}⁡y+{C}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{ln}^{2}⁡y+{C}_{2} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {ln}^{2}⁡y & =-{x}^{2}+2({C}_{1}-{C}_{2}) \\ {ln}^{2}⁡y & =C-{x}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2({C}_{1}-{C}_{2})$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(0)=e$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{ln}^{2}⁡e & =C-{0}^{2} \\ {1}^{2} & =C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So we get the particular solution in implicit form:

$$
{ln}^{2}⁡y=1-{x}^{2}.
$$

content.worked_solution:

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{xy}{\operatorname{ln}⁡y} \\ \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-x \\ \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =-\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\,\text{d}y & =-\int x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\text{d}y & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate the integral in the left-hand side of this equality, we use a substitution $u=\operatorname{ln}⁡y.$ Then,  we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=\frac{1}{y}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y.
$$

So we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}{y}\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{ln}⁡y(\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\int u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{u}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{ln}^{2}⁡y+{C}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{ln}^{2}⁡y+{C}_{2} & =-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1} \\ {ln}^{2}⁡y & =-{x}^{2}+2({C}_{1}-{C}_{2}) \\ {ln}^{2}⁡y & =C-{x}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2({C}_{1}-{C}_{2})$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now apply the condition $y(0)=e$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{ln}^{2}⁡e & =C-{0}^{2} \\ {1}^{2} & =C \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Find the particular solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{e}^{-y}=3{x}^{2}{e}^{-y}$ that satisfies $y(1)=1.$
after.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{e}^{-y} & =3{x}^{2}{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}{e}^{-y}-2x{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(3{x}^{2}-2x){e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}-2x \\ \int {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (3{x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & ={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{3}-{1}^{2}+C) & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡C & =1 \\ C & =e\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{e}^{-y}=3{x}^{2}{e}^{-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+e).
$$

We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{e}^{-y} & =3{x}^{2}{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}{e}^{-y}-2x{e}^{-y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(3{x}^{2}-2x){e}^{-y} \\ {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}-2x \\ \int {e}^{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ \int {e}^{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int (3{x}^{2}-2x)\,\text{d}x \\ {e}^{y} & ={x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the natural logarithm to both sides, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+C) \\ y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+C)\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(1)=1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(1) & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{3}-{1}^{2}+C) & =1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡C & =1 \\ C & =e\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the particular solution of $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2x{e}^{-y}=3{x}^{2}{e}^{-y}$ that satisfies the condition $y(1)=1$ is

$$
y=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+e).
$$

content.worked_solution:
We first find the general solution and then apply the given initial condition to find a particular solution.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}+{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={y}^{2}(\frac{4}{{x}^{2}}+1) \\ \frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =(4{x}^{-2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{-2}\,\text{d}y & =\int (4{x}^{-2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\ -{y}^{-1} & =-4{x}^{-1}+x+C \\ -\frac{1}{y} & =-\frac{4}{x}+x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for $y$, we find the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{y} & =\frac{4}{x}-x-C \\ \frac{1}{y} & =\frac{4-{x}^{2}-Cx}{x} \\ y & =\frac{x}{4-{x}^{2}-Cx}\end{aligned}
$$

We now apply the initial condition $y(2)=-1$ to find $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2) & =-1 \\ \frac{2}{4-{2}^{2}-C(2)} & =-1 \\ \frac{2}{-2C} & =-1 \\ -\frac{1}{C} & =-1 \\ C & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the particular solution is

$$
y(x)=\frac{x}{4-x-{x}^{2}}.
$$
